items.stem: What does it mean for an Ansible task to be idempotent?

options.text: Running it repeatedly leaves the system in the same final state without needless changes
options.rationale: Correct: idempotent tasks only change what is not already in the desired state.

options.text: It can only ever be run once
options.rationale: Idempotency is about safe repetition, not one-time use.

options.text: It always reports changed on every run
options.rationale: A truly idempotent task reports ok when nothing needs changing.

options.text: It requires an agent on each node
options.rationale: Ansible is agentless; idempotency is unrelated to agents.

items.explanation: Correct: idempotent tasks only change what is not already in the desired state.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO correctly describe Ansible handlers? (Select TWO)

options.text: A handler runs only when notified by a task that reported changed
options.rationale: Correct: handlers fire on notification from a changed task.

options.text: Handlers typically run once at the end of a play
options.rationale: Correct: notified handlers run after tasks, usually at the play's end.

options.text: Handlers run on every task regardless of changes

options.rationale: Restarting a service is a classic handler use.

items.explanation: Correct: handlers fire on notification from a changed task.

items.stem: Why is Ansible described as agentless?

options.text: It connects to managed nodes over SSH and does not require installed daemons
options.rationale: Correct: Ansible pushes over SSH (or WinRM) without a persistent agent on nodes.

options.text: It never connects to any remote host
options.rationale: It does connect, just without an agent.

options.text: It only configures the control node
It requires a kernel module on each host

items.explanation: Correct: Ansible pushes over SSH (or WinRM) without a persistent agent on nodes.
